sm: The host, from the Cross Politic show, reflects on the November third elections in Texas, where Democrats flipped the governor's race, the Senate, lieutenant governor, attorney general and the House. He lays the blame mostly on Governor Abbott rather than Trump, saying Abbott campaigned for years on lowering property taxes and never did it. He contrasts Abbott with Ron DeSantis, who grew his support by leading with courage. He says Republicans with majorities get nothing done, such as the Save Act, and he holds up Charlie Kirk as a leader who pulled people along by standing out in front. He closes by urging Christians to be neither so heavenly minded they are no earthly good, nor carnally minded.

The host says Christians should be spiritually minded and engaged, like Christ healing the leper rather than catching leprosy. He cites a friend, Joseph Backholm, who said that if eighty percent of Seattle's churchgoers voted, the city council would be Christianized. He notes the evangelical vote dropped to seventeen percent this election, and says the church's apathy is the real problem. He then introduces his guest, Brent Money, a Republican Texas state representative for House District 2, a Greenville native and attorney, just re-elected. Money says the host is largely right but undervalues the Trump effect. He says a fourth term for any governor is a bad idea, suggests term limits for governor and lieutenant governor might win bipartisan support, and calls Ken Paxton a great attorney general who is unlikable to independents.

Money says Paxton's personal and marital baggage, including a publicized adulterous relationship during his Senate run, hurt him with voters. He says Abbott had been in office too long, and Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick grew out of touch by pushing subsidies for the movie industry, a state-funded Alzheimer's research effort, and a crackdown on THC that upset veterans. He adds that importing Argentinian beef angered Texas ranchers. He argues that Republican wins have mostly been stopping the left's worst ideas, while affordability, housing and small business have been neglected. The host replies that he is not against term limits in principle, but he wants a good governor to stay, and he compares Abbott to Idaho's Governor Little, a corporatist.

Money says Texas voters could have dumped Abbott in the 2022 primary but didn't, and that Abbott's third term was his best, though too late. He says people are also frustrated with Congress, which hasn't codified Trump's border and Doge actions or passed the Save America Act. The host says Abbott's budget grew about four percent a year per person while Florida's grew about two percent. The host also notes Texas has roughly twenty-five thousand Christian churches, and he says Republican old-guard leaders want power for a country club rather than an agenda. He also says Abbott, the lieutenant governor and the attorney general deserve what they got, with no accountability coming.

Money says Texas has won the best state for business award thirteen years running, but asks how that helped longtime residents, since wages are flat while property taxes, traffic and crime rose. He says about eighteen percent of Texans were born abroad, and that Indian Americans, whom Abbott courted, voted about eighty percent Democratic. He argues Texas should have asserted its sovereignty on the border and stopped rewarding companies that use foreign labor. The host notes Abbott's vote total stayed near four and a half million while Democrats gained two million votes, and asks about voter registration growth. Money says election integrity claims should be examined seriously without scapegoating, and that more is needed to shore up the system.

Asked if Texas will turn red again, Money says yes, calling the result a repudiation of Washington and Austin rather than of conservative policy. He points out that bond measures failed, and that voters still agree with Republicans on core issues but are angry about the economy. He expects two to four years of legislative gridlock, with Republicans holding the Senate eighteen to ten and Democrats the House. He says Republicans need better candidates and a positive message, not just attacks on Democrats. He cites Congressman Brandon Gill winning by double digits in the same district James Talarico also won by double digits. The host describes Idaho, where only Lava County grew redder, and says the long game is faithful families and having children.

Money says most people ignore politics until election time, so Christians must disciple people year round, recruit better candidates, and build grassroots organization with door knocking, since Democrats beat Republicans on ground game. Asked about 2028, he says he is no national pundit, but expects JD Vance, Ron DeSantis, Glenn Youngkin, Ted Cruz and perhaps Tom Cotton to run. He thinks Marco Rubio will not run against Vance, and notes that Pete Hegseth has been mentioned. He says the Republican bench is deep and voters are fickle. The host closes by urging Christians to care about politics without anxiety, trusting the Lord rather than chariots and horses, and to focus on what they directly control, their family, home, job and neighborhood.
